Rust has no classes and no inheritance. It has structs (data), enums (data that is one of several shapes), traits (shared behaviour, module 02.05) and composition. This combination is why Rust code tends to have small, obvious types.

Structs

Named fields

Field init shorthand and struct update

..base moves non-Copy fields out of base. After that, base is partially moved and cannot be used as a whole.

Tuple structs

The newtype pattern: a one-field tuple struct that gives a distinct type to a primitive. It prevents passing a UserId where a u64 order id is expected, at zero runtime cost.

Now any function taking Email is guaranteed a validated address. This is the single most valuable pattern in Rust application code.

Unit structs

Used for type-state and as trait impl targets.

impl blocks

Self is an alias for the type being implemented. impl Into<String> accepts both &str and String without a generic parameter at the call site.

Multiple impl blocks

Legal and useful: keep inherent methods separate from trait impls, or split by feature flag.

Builder pattern

Rust has no named/default arguments, so builders are the idiomatic answer for anything with more than ~4 fields.

Taking mut self and returning Self makes the chain work by value. The derive(Default) on the builder means every field has a sane starting point.

Gotcha: if the builder's build() validates, do not also offer Default on the built type — two ways to construct an invalid value defeats the point.

Enums

An enum is a type that is exactly one of a fixed set of variants, and each variant may carry data. This replaces the C "tag + union" pattern and makes illegal states unrepresentable.

match self on &self binds radius: &f64 — match ergonomics dereference automatically. No * needed to read it.

Option<T> and Result<T, E> are ordinary enums

There is no null in Rust. Option<T> costs nothing extra when T is a non-nullable pointer (Option<Box<T>> is pointer-sized), because the niche optimisation stores None in the null bit pattern.

Pattern matching in depth

Patterns everywhere

Pattern syntax reference

Pattern Matches
_ anything, binds nothing
x anything, binds to x
1 / 'a' / "s" a literal
1..=5 / 'a'..='z' a range (integers, chars)
A | B either
Some(x) a variant, binding its payload
Point { x, y: 0 } a struct with a field pattern
Point { x, .. } a struct, ignoring the rest
[a, b, ..] a slice with at least two elements
(a, b) a tuple
ref x / &x bind by reference / destructure a reference
x @ 1..=9 bind and test
NAME a unit struct or const — not a new binding

Use a path (Self::MAX) or a literal to compare. Clippy warns about bindings_with_variant_name.

Destructuring with .. and nested patterns

matches! macro

Much cleaner than if let ... { true } else { false }.

Methods on enums: the state machine pattern

Taking self and returning State makes transitions explicit and total.

Default, From, TryFrom

From/TryFrom give you .into() / .try_into() for free, and they compose with generic APIs.

Exercises

  1. Add a Scale(f64) variant to Shape that scales every other shape. Decide whether Scale should be a variant or a method — justify it.
  2. Implement Email as a validated newtype and use it in a User struct. Confirm no code path can construct an invalid Email.
  3. Write fn classify(input: &str) -> Token with at least five variants including one carrying data, and a Display impl.
  4. Build a ServerConfigBuilder with a build() that rejects port 0. Add a test for the rejection.
